item.title: Cisco IOS and IOS-XE Upgrade Guide: Catalyst Switches and ISR Routers
item.description: Step-by-step Cisco IOS and IOS-XE software upgrade for Catalyst switches (2960, 3560, 3850, 9200, 9300, 9500) and routers (ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8000) — flash checks, ROMMON, install mode, bundle mode, MD5 and rollback.
item.content:encoded:
Most Cisco upgrades fail before the first command is typed: the wrong image for the platform, too little space in flash, a ROMMON that is too old for the target release, or a boot variable that points nowhere. This guide puts the checks first and the commands second.

It covers both families you meet in practice:

Family Typical models Software File system Upgrade method
Classic Catalyst switches 2960, 2960-X, 3560, 3750 IOS flash: archive download-sw or .bin + boot system
IOS-XE Catalyst switches 3650, 3850, 9200, 9300, 9400, 9500 IOS-XE flash: (on some models bootflash:) Install mode (packages.conf)
IOS-XE routers ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8200/8300, Catalyst 8000V IOS-XE bootflash: Install mode or bundle mode
Classic IOS routers ISR G2, C900 IOS flash: .bin + boot system

The commands are the ones I use in the field on Catalyst switches and ISR routers. IP addresses and paths in the examples are placeholders.

1. Check the Platform Before Anything Else

File System: flash: or bootflash:?

Do not assume. Ask the device:

show file systems
dir

Classic Catalyst switches and Catalyst 9200/9300 use flash:. ISR and Catalyst 8000 routers use bootflash:. On many IOS-XE platforms one name is an alias for the other. Use whatever the device shows. Every command in this guide works with either name.

Model, Version and Boot Mode

show version
show inventory
show boot            ! switches
show bootvar         ! routers
show install summary ! IOS-XE only

Write down:

  • Exact model and platform family. An image for an ISR 4300 does not boot on an ISR 4400. The platform family is in the file name, for example isr4300-universalk9, c1100-universalk9, cat9k_iosxe.
  • Current version.
  • Boot mode on IOS-XE. If the boot variable points to packages.conf, the device runs in install mode. If it points to a .bin file, it runs in bundle mode.

Free Space

dir shows the free bytes at the bottom. An IOS-XE image is large, and install mode needs extra space to extract the packages. If space is tight, clean up first:

install remove inactive   ! IOS-XE install mode: removes unused packages
delete flash:<old-image>.bin

2. Read the Release Notes: Upgrade Path and ROMMON

Two things in the release notes decide whether the upgrade works:

  • Upgrade path. Some jumps are not supported directly. Cisco documents, for example, that Catalyst 9500 switches in bundle mode should go from 16.x to 17.x through an intermediate release, while install mode supports the direct jump.
  • Minimum ROMMON version. Every IOS-XE release needs a minimum ROMMON (boot loader) version. If the device has an older ROMMON, the new image may not boot and the device stops at the rommon prompt.

Check the current ROMMON version:

show rom-monitor r0          ! ISR 4000 and similar routers
show version | include ROM   ! most platforms

Does ROMMON Need a Separate Upgrade?

  • Catalyst 9000: Usually not by hand. When a new release contains a newer ROMMON, the switch upgrades its primary ROMMON automatically at the first boot. The golden (backup) ROMMON is upgraded manually with the upgrade rom-monitor capsule golden command. The exact arguments differ by model, so check the upgrade guide for your platform.
  • ISR 4000 and similar routers: Check it every time. A well-known case is ISR 4000 routers that need ROMMON 16.12(2r) before they boot 17.x releases.

Upgrading ROMMON on an ISR 4000

ROMMON is upgraded from the running IOS-XE, not from the ROMMON prompt. Copy the ROMMON package, verify it, then:

copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/isr4200_4300_rommon_1612_2r_SPA.pkg bootflash:
verify /md5 bootflash:isr4200_4300_rommon_1612_2r_SPA.pkg
upgrade rom-monitor filename bootflash:isr4200_4300_rommon_1612_2r_SPA.pkg R0
reload
show rom-monitor r0

Do the ROMMON upgrade before the software upgrade. If you get it wrong and the device no longer boots, see Cisco ROMMON Recovery.

Secure Boot and Signed Images

IOS-XE images are signed. The .SPA in the file name stands for a signed production image. The device verifies the signature at boot. An image for the wrong platform or a corrupted file fails this check and does not boot. Only use images from Cisco Software Download and always verify the checksum.

3. Copy the Image and Verify It

FTP is faster and more reliable than TFTP for large IOS-XE images:

copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/isr4300-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin bootflash:
copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/c1100-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin bootflash:
copy tftp://192.0.2.10/cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin flash:

Setting up the server, credentials, the double slash in FTP paths and the management VRF are covered in TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades.

Verify the MD5 checksum against the value on the Cisco download page:

verify /md5 bootflash:c1100-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin

If the values differ, delete the file and copy it again. Never install an image that failed verification.

4. Upgrade in Install Mode (IOS-XE)

Install mode is the recommended mode for Catalyst 9000 switches and current ISR and Catalyst 8000 routers. One command adds, activates and commits the new software:

install add file bootflash:isr4300-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin activate commit

The device asks whether it may reload. Answer y. After the reload:

show version
show install summary
install remove inactive

show install summary should show the new version as Committed. install remove inactive removes the old packages and frees space.

On Catalyst 9000 switches the command is the same, with the switch file system:

install add file flash:cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin activate commit

Several Hops in a Row

If the release notes require an intermediate release, repeat the sequence per hop: copy, verify, install add ... activate commit, check, install remove inactive. For example 17.9 first, then 17.12. Clean up between the hops so there is room for the next image.

From Bundle Mode to Install Mode

A device in bundle mode boots a .bin file directly. To switch to install mode:

  1. Run install add file <image>.bin activate commit as above. This extracts the packages and creates packages.conf.
  2. Make sure the boot variable points to packages.conf:
configure terminal
no boot system
boot system flash:packages.conf
end
write memory
show boot

On routers, use bootflash:packages.conf.

5. Bundle Mode and Classic IOS

IOS-XE in Bundle Mode, ISR G2, C900

configure terminal
no boot system
boot system bootflash:<image>.bin
end
write memory
show bootvar
reload

On classic IOS routers like the C900 series, the file system is flash: and the image name has the old format, for example c900-universalk9-mz.SPA.<version>.bin.

Classic Catalyst Switches (2960, 3560, 3750)

These switches offer archive download-sw. It transfers a .tar file, extracts it, sets the boot variable and can reload:

archive download-sw /overwrite /reload tftp://192.0.2.10/c3560-ipservicesk9-tar.<version>.tar
  • /overwrite replaces the current image when flash has room for only one.
  • /leave-old-sw keeps the old image when there is room for both. Rollback is then just a boot variable change.

Alternatively, copy the .bin file, verify it and set boot system flash:<image>.bin as above.

6. After the Upgrade

show version
show install summary          ! IOS-XE install mode
show interfaces status        ! switches
show ip interface brief
show power inline             ! PoE switches
show logging

On stacks and redundant systems, check every member: show switch on Catalyst stacks, show redundancy on dual-supervisor systems.

7. Rollback

  • Install mode: show install rollback lists the rollback points.
  • Bundle mode and classic IOS: point boot system back to the old image, if it is still in flash, and reload.
  • Device stops at ROMMON or the switch: prompt: see Cisco ROMMON Recovery.

Common Mistakes

  • Image for the wrong platform family. It fails signature or platform checks and does not boot.
  • ROMMON not checked. The new image needs a newer ROMMON, and the device stops at the rommon prompt.
  • No space for install mode. The extraction fails halfway. Run install remove inactive first.
  • Boot variable still points to the old .bin after moving to install mode. The device boots the old version in bundle mode.
  • No console access during the reload. A console server makes this possible remotely: Next-Gen Console Server Architecture.

Related Articles

  • Cisco ROMMON Recovery: Boot from Flash, TFTP or USB
  • TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades
  • Cisco Switch and Router Password Recovery
  • Cisco Nexus NX-OS Software Upgrade Guide

Sources: Cisco: Upgrading Catalyst 9500 Switches · Cisco: Upgrading Catalyst 9300 Switches

item.title: Cisco Switch and Router Password Recovery: Catalyst 9000, 2960, 3560 and ISR
item.description: Recover a lost enable or console password on Cisco devices without losing the configuration — classic Catalyst (2960, 3560, 3750), Catalyst 9000 and 3850 with SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG, ISR routers with confreg 0x2142, and what to do when password recovery is disabled.
item.content:encoded:
You inherit a device without documentation, or a lab switch comes back from storage and asks for a password nobody knows. On Cisco switches and routers you can recover from this without losing the configuration, as long as you have physical access and a console cable.

The principle is the same everywhere: interrupt the boot, start IOS without loading the startup configuration, then put the configuration back and set new passwords. Only the way you tell the device to skip the configuration differs:

Platform Typical models How the configuration is skipped
Classic Catalyst 2960, 2960-X, 3560, 3750 Rename config.text in the boot loader
IOS-XE Catalyst 3650, 3850, 9200, 9300, 9400, 9500 SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG=1
Routers ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8000, ISR G2 Configuration register 0x2142

What You Need

  • Physical access to the device, or a console server. Password recovery is deliberately not possible over the network. See Next-Gen Console Server Architecture.
  • A console cable and a terminal program. Settings: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control.
  • A maintenance window. The device reboots and does not forward traffic during the procedure.

Switches: Get to the switch: Prompt

On Catalyst switches you interrupt the boot with the Mode button:

  1. Connect the console and open the terminal session.
  2. Unplug the power.
  3. Hold the Mode button on the front panel and reconnect the power.
  4. Keep holding until the console shows that the boot was interrupted, about 10 to 15 seconds, then release.

You are now at the switch: prompt.

On a Catalyst 9400 with two supervisors, Cisco recommends removing the secondary supervisor before you start.

Classic Catalyst (2960, 3560, 3750): Rename config.text

switch: flash_init
switch: dir flash:
switch: rename flash:config.text flash:config.text.old
switch: boot

Some older boot loaders also need load_helper after flash_init. Do not delete config.text. Renaming is enough, and you need the contents later.

The switch boots without configuration. Answer no to the initial configuration dialog, then:

Switch> enable
Switch# rename flash:config.text.old flash:config.text
Switch# copy flash:config.text system:running-config

Continue with the section “Set New Passwords and Save” below.

Catalyst 9000 and 3850: SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG

IOS-XE switches do not need the rename. A boot loader variable tells IOS to ignore the startup configuration:

switch: SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG=1
switch: boot flash:packages.conf

Use boot flash:<image>.bin if the switch runs in bundle mode. After the boot, answer no to the initial configuration dialog, then load the configuration:

Switch> enable
Switch# copy startup-config running-config

Important: reset the variable from IOS. Otherwise the switch ignores its configuration at every reload:

Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# no system ignore startupconfig switch all
Switch(config)# end

Continue with the next section, then save.

Routers (ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8000): confreg 0x2142

Routers do not have a Mode button. Interrupt the boot by sending a Break from the terminal program during the first seconds after power-on. You land at the rommon 1 > prompt.

rommon 1 > confreg 0x2142
rommon 2 > reset

The value 0x2142 tells the router to ignore the startup configuration. After the boot, answer no to the initial configuration dialog:

Router> enable
Router# copy startup-config running-config
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# config-register 0x2102

Setting the register back to 0x2102 is essential. Otherwise the router ignores its configuration at every reload.

Set New Passwords and Save

You are now in privileged mode with the original configuration loaded. Set new credentials to match how authentication was set up before:

configure terminal
enable secret <new-enable-secret>
username admin privilege 15 secret <new-password>
line con 0
 login local
line vty 0 15
 login local
end

If the device uses TACACS+ or RADIUS, check that the local fallback account works.

Copying a configuration into the running configuration merges it. Interfaces may stay administratively down, especially VLAN interfaces (SVIs) on switches. Check and fix:

show ip interface brief

Bring up interfaces that should be up with no shutdown. Then save and test:

write memory
reload

Log in with the new credentials after the reload to confirm that the configuration and the passwords survive.

When Password Recovery Is Disabled

If no service password-recovery is configured, the procedure behaves differently. The device does not let you skip the configuration. Instead it says that password recovery is disabled and asks whether to reset to the factory default configuration.

  • Yes: the configuration (and on switches the VLAN database) is deleted. The device boots with default settings. The IOS image stays.
  • No: the device boots normally with the current configuration, and you are back at the password prompt.

This is the purpose of the feature. Someone with physical access cannot read the configuration, but you lose it too. Before you answer yes, make sure you have a recent configuration backup from another source. After the reset, restore the configuration and recreate the VLANs if the backup does not contain them.

no service password-recovery makes sense for devices in public or unlocked locations, as long as the configuration is backed up somewhere else.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting config.text instead of renaming it. Only a backup helps then.
  • Forgetting no system ignore startupconfig switch all or config-register 0x2102. The device boots without configuration at the next reload.
  • Not saving after setting the passwords. The old passwords come back at the next reload.
  • SVIs left shut down after the merge. Management access over the network fails although the configuration looks correct.

Related Articles

  • Cisco ROMMON Recovery: Boot from Flash, TFTP or USB
  • Cisco IOS and IOS-XE Upgrade Guide
  • Next-Gen Console Server Architecture

Source: Cisco: Troubleshoot Bootloader and Password Recovery on Catalyst 9000

item.title: TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades: Setup and Troubleshooting
item.description: How to set up a TFTP, FTP or SCP server for Cisco IOS and IOS-XE image transfers on Windows, macOS and Linux — device-side commands, the management VRF, the FTP double-slash path, file size limits and firewall issues.
item.content:encoded:
Every Cisco upgrade starts with getting a file onto the device. For a 20 MB classic IOS image, almost anything works. For a 1 GB IOS-XE image over a WAN link, the choice of protocol decides whether the copy takes five minutes or fails after an hour.

This guide covers which protocol to use, how to set up the server on Windows, macOS and Linux, and the device-side commands and pitfalls.

Which Protocol?

Protocol Port Authentication Strengths Weaknesses
TFTP UDP 69 None Simple, supported everywhere, works from ROMMON Slow, unreliable over WAN, size limits on old servers
FTP TCP 21 (+ data) User and password Fast and reliable for large images Clear text, needs firewall handling for the data channel
SCP TCP 22 SSH Encrypted, uses existing SSH access Slower than FTP on some platforms
HTTP(S) TCP 80/443 Optional Fast, easy to host Not available on older IOS versions

My rule in practice:

  • FTP for normal upgrades over the network. It is fast and reliable for large IOS-XE images.
  • TFTP when the device is in ROMMON. ROMMON can only do TFTP. See Cisco ROMMON Recovery.
  • SCP when the security policy does not allow clear-text protocols.

Server Setup

Windows: Tftpd64

Tftpd64 is a free tool that combines a TFTP server, a DHCP server and a syslog server.

  1. Install Tftpd64 and start it.
  2. Set the Current Directory to the folder that contains your images.
  3. Select the Server interface, the IP address of the network adapter that faces the devices.
  4. Allow Tftpd64 in the Windows firewall. This is the most common reason why transfers time out.

For FTP on Windows, FileZilla Server is a common free choice.

macOS: Built-in TFTP Server

macOS has a TFTP server on board. It serves files from /private/tftpboot:

sudo mkdir -p /private/tftpboot
sudo cp <image>.bin /private/tftpboot/
sudo chmod 644 /private/tftpboot/<image>.bin
sudo launchctl load -F /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/tftp.plist

Stop it again with sudo launchctl unload -F /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/tftp.plist. If the macOS firewall is active, allow incoming connections.

Linux: tftpd-hpa and vsftpd

On Debian and Ubuntu:

sudo apt install tftpd-hpa

The configuration is in /etc/default/tftpd-hpa. The default directory is /srv/tftp:

TFTP_DIRECTORY="/srv/tftp"
TFTP_OPTIONS="--secure"

Add --create to TFTP_OPTIONS only if devices should be able to upload files, for example configuration backups.

For FTP, vsftpd with a local user is enough:

sudo apt install vsftpd
sudo adduser netops

Put the images in the user’s home directory or in a shared directory such as /tftpboot/images.

Device Side: Copying the Image

TFTP

copy tftp://192.0.2.10/<image>.bin flash:

FTP

Credentials can be part of the URL, or configured once:

configure terminal
ip ftp username netops
ip ftp password <password>
end
copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/<image>.bin bootflash:

The double slash. In an FTP URL, IOS treats the path as relative to the FTP user’s home directory. If the images are in an absolute path outside the home directory, use two slashes after the server address:

copy ftp://192.0.2.10//tftpboot/images/<image>.bin bootflash:

ftp://server/images/file means <home>/images/file. ftp://server//tftpboot/images/file means /tftpboot/images/file. This detail explains many “file not found” errors.

SCP

Pulling a file from an SCP server:

copy scp://netops@192.0.2.10/images/<image>.bin flash:

Pushing a file to the device from your laptop requires the SCP server on the device:

configure terminal
ip scp server enable
end

Then from the laptop:

scp <image>.bin admin@<device-ip>:flash:<image>.bin

Disable ip scp server enable again after the transfer if your policy requires it.

Always Verify

verify /md5 flash:<image>.bin

Compare the value with the MD5 checksum on the Cisco download page. A file that copied without errors can still be incomplete.

The Management Port and VRF

On Catalyst 9000 switches, the dedicated management port (GigabitEthernet0/0) sits in its own VRF called Mgmt-vrf. On ISR 4000 and Catalyst 8000 routers, the management port is in the VRF Mgmt-intf. A copy without a VRF uses the global routing table and fails if the server is only reachable through the management network.

Tell the device which interface to use as the source:

configure terminal
ip tftp source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
ip ftp source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
end

The router management port is named GigabitEthernet0 on ISR 4000 routers. Check the name with show ip interface brief.

Troubleshooting

Timeout or “Connection refused”

  • ping the server from the device, with the right source interface or VRF.
  • Check the firewall on the server. Windows and macOS block incoming connections by default.
  • For FTP: the data channel uses additional ports. If a firewall sits between device and server, passive mode problems are common.

“File not found”

  • Check the path relative to the server’s root directory (TFTP) or the user’s home directory (FTP). Remember the double slash.
  • Check upper and lower case. File names are case-sensitive on Linux and macOS servers.
  • Check that the server user can read the file.

Copy Stops at 32 MB (TFTP)

Classic TFTP uses 512-byte blocks and a 16-bit block counter. That limits a transfer to about 32 MB unless both sides support larger blocks or block number rollover. Old or minimal TFTP servers still have this limit. IOS-XE images are much larger.

  • Use FTP or SCP for large images.
  • If you must use TFTP, use a current server and increase the block size on the device:
configure terminal
ip tftp blocksize 8192
end

Very Slow Transfer

TFTP waits for an acknowledgment after every block. Over a WAN link with high latency, that makes it extremely slow. Use FTP or SCP over long distances, or place a server close to the device.
